title: North Carolina Democrats Propose Changes to Block GOP Power Transfers and Secrecy
author: Doug Bock Clark
content:
Democratic lawmakers in North Carolina introduced a trio of constitutional
amendments this week aimed at protecting traditional powers of the state’s
governor and reforming oversight of its court system.

The effort was prompted in part by [ProPublica’s reporting, including an
investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/north-carolina-governor-
power-transfers-gop) that found that over nearly a decade, Republican
lawmakers had pushed through law after law shrinking the powers of North
Carolina’s governor, always a Democrat during that time.

At a press conference on Wednesday, the bills’ sponsors readily acknowledged
that the initiatives are unlikely to pass, at least in the current legislative
session: Republicans hold majorities in North Carolina’s House and Senate.

But in proposing the measures as changes to the state constitution, the group
of eight Democrats said their goal was to make them less vulnerable to the
persistent partisan warfare that has engulfed the narrowly divided swing
state.

Republicans “won’t always be in the majority,” said Rep. Phil Rubin, the
primary sponsor of [one
bill](https://webservices.ncleg.gov/ViewBillDocument/2025/9284/0/DRH10656-MCy-333).
“And when they’re not, they’re going to suddenly think these are great rules.
So let’s do them now.”

Republican leaders in the House, Senate and court system did not respond to
requests for comment on the bills.

Experts have long maintained that Republican power grabs have thwarted the
will of North Carolina voters, removing the Democratic governor’s control or
partial control over numerous boards, entities and executive prerogatives and
leaving him the nation’s weakest. (Republican officials have defended the
shifts, pointing out that voters also elected a GOP legislative majority.)

Rubin’s measure would bar the legislature from stripping away additional
gubernatorial powers, as well as block majority leaders from what he called
“government by ambush” — springing major legislation on the minority and
public without notice.

“ProPublica’s reporting shows the perils of not having this law,” Rubin said.
Voters should have “the opportunity to secure their constitution, demand
absolute transparency in lawmaking and ensure that people, not backroom deals,
have the final say.”

The two other constitutional amendments unveiled this week target aspects of
the judicial system.

[The
first](https://webservices.ncleg.gov/ViewBillDocument/2025/9285/0/DRH40737-NQy-59%27),
authored by House Rep. Marcia Morey, would make disciplinary hearings and
sanctions by the courts’ internal watchdog, the Judicial Standards Commission,
public.

GOP rules currently cloak the commission’s work in secrecy. Behind closed
doors, [ProPublica revealed](https://www.propublica.org/article/north-
carolina-supreme-court-republican-judges-violations), the majority-Republican
state Supreme Court quashed the commission’s recommendations that two
Republican judges who’d admitted to committing egregious conduct violations be
publicly reprimanded. (Spokespeople for the North Carolina Supreme Court and
the Judicial Standards Commission declined to comment or respond to a detailed
list of questions about the matter.)

Morey’s bill would also change who appoints the commission’s members, a step
she called critical to preventing the “weaponization” of its work.

Currently, Republican legislative leaders and Paul Newby, the state’s
conservative chief justice, appoint a majority of the commission’s members. As
[ProPublica has reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/north-carolina-
supreme-court-republican-judges-violations), in 2023 Newby encouraged the
commission to investigate a Black Democratic justice who’d criticized his
decision to effectively shut down a racial equity commission. (Newby, as well
as spokespeople for the court and the Judicial Standards Commission, declined
to comment for the story.)

Morey’s measure would divide commission appointments equally among the chief
justice, the governor and the North Carolina State Bar. “Who makes decisions
about discipline and who appoints the decision-makers,” she said, are critical
to making the system “fair and effective.”

The [second
bill](https://webservices.ncleg.gov/ViewBillDocument/2025/9283/0/DRH40738-NQy-34),
sponsored by Rep. Deb Butler, would disqualify state Supreme Court justices
from hearing cases in which family members are parties. Justice Phil Berger
Jr. has [caused controversy](https://ncnewsline.com/2024/08/29/democrats-
renew-calls-for-supreme-court-justice-to-recuse-himself-from-cases-involving-
his-father/) by [ruling in multiple cases](https://www.wral.com/story/north-
carolina-supreme-court-dismisses-motion-asking-justice-to-recuse-from-leandro-
lawsuit-involving-father/21287748/) in which his father, the leader of the
state Senate, is a defendant in his legislative capacity. (Berger [referred
recusal requests](https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-
government/article291371665.html) on these cases to the Republican majority on
the Supreme Court, which [ruled he could
participate](https://appellate.nccourts.org/orders.php?t=P&court=1&id=435695&pdf=1&a=0&docket=1&dev=1).)

Butler’s measure would also compel justices to disclose more information about
large stock transactions, outside sources of income and sponsored travel. A
ProPublica [investigation found
Newby](https://www.propublica.org/article/paul-newby-north-carolina-supreme-
court) didn’t disclose a trip to a luxurious Hawaiian resort, paid for by a
conservative judicial education program. Newby and court spokespeople did not
respond to requests for comment about his decision not to disclose the trip.

Butler described her bill as an effort to restore public trust. “People
deserve complete confidence in the integrity of their court,” she said.

In the unlikely event that the bills pass, the public would then have the
chance to vote on them in November. If not, the sponsors said, they’d revive
them in the next session, by which time even [some Republican
strategists](https://www.wunc.org/politics/2026-06-03/blue-wave-nc-democrats-
flip-majority-legislature-house-senate) think that a blue wave may have
flipped the North Carolina House.

“We’re committed to following through on these bills to ensure fairness and
impartiality in our courts and legislature,” Morey said. “This should be the
norm, not the partisan bias we have now.”
